label: text
text: PLAIN SPEAKING RESENTED:

label: paragraph_title
text: London, October 12:

label: text
text: In spite of the opposition of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, and Mr. J. H. Thomas, who pointed out the unpracticability, the Labour Party Conference at Margate carried by a majority of over three million a resolution recognising the magnificent resistance of the miners and urging the nationalisation of the mines, condemning the coal mines which extend the working day and generally giving effect to the South Wales drastic resolution adopted at the 'Miners' Delegate Conference.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: ANIMATED SCENES.

label: paragraph_title
text: Proposed Levy Attacked:

label: text
text:
Rugby, October 12.
There were more animated scenes when the annual conference of the Labour Party was continued at Margate to-day.

label: text
text: Mr. Rhys Davies, Member of Parliament, moved a resolution protesting against the manner in which the Government had handled the could crisis, and expressing the opinion that the deep-rooted and urgent problems of the mining industry could only be settled by the adoption of a scheme of nationalisation.

label: text
text: This resolution was strongly attacked by a number of speakers on the ground that it gave no practical support to the miners.

label: text
text: Mr. David Kirkwood, a prominent member of the Labour Party's left wing, wanted a resolution with some "kick" in it, which would encourage the brave men and women in the capital fields. What miners now required, he said, was money. He asked for a levy on all the affiliated Unions.

label: text
text: Mr. Horne, delegate of the South Wales miners, declared: "We don't want your empty resolution. If you would help us, let us have money and an embargo."

label: text
text: Mr. J. H. Thomas, Railwaymen's Leader, who was Colonial Secretary

label: figure_title
text: Mr. J. H. Thomas, M.P.

label: text
text: in the late Labour Government, said that he would tell the conference why a levy on other Trades Unions to help the miners was impossible. At this moment there were 45,000 railwaymen who had never gone back to work since the general strike of last May. In addition 200,000 railwaymen were only working three days a week. The Engineers' Union was now taking a levy for its own men. In the Boilermakers' Union 45 per cent of the men were unemployed.

label: text
text: As to an embargo on foreign coal, Mr. Thomas declared that the resolution recently passed by the International Miners Federation at Brussels favouring the prevention of the export of coal to Great Britain was only a piece of paper. It was no use to deceive the miners by talk about an embargo, which could not be realised.

label: text
text: Mr. Thomas's plain truths were received with angry shouts and much interruption by the extremist section of the conference.

label: text
text:
Situation Not Realised.
Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald, Leader of the Labour Party, emphasised the impossibility of a Trade Union levy. He said that the situation was not adequately realised. There had been a consultation with the Union leaders as to the best means of helping the miners, and he had been perfectly appalled at the unemployment in each Union. The industrial situation had to be faced. The resolution before the conference definitely committed the Parliamentary Labour Party to nationalisation of mines, and he hoped that the conference would pass it and thus give some encouragement to the miners. It was the best thing that the conference could do now. The miners' fight would only begin on a new plane when the present crisis was over. That new plane was the House of Commons and the new policy was nationalisation of industry.

label: text
text: Mr. MacDonald's statements evoked some booing.

label: text
text: Eventually the resolution was adopted by an overwhelming majority of 3,315,000 votes against 210,000.—British Wireless Service. Safety Men Move.

label: text
text:
London, October 12.
While the miners of the respective districts are considering the proposals of the Miners' Federation Conference to call out the safety men from the pits, the latter themselves are taking action.

label: text
text: A deputation of the Federation, Colliery Deputies and Firemen's Associations representing 30,000 safety men were received at the Ministry of Labour, and discussed the situation with Sir Arthur Maitland to whom they submitted their position. The deputies were refused unemployment benefit during the stoppage.

label: text
text:
Simultaneously the National Executive of this Federation met and urged that the time had come to reach a settlement. It is understood that the Federation adheres to its policy of advising the safety men to remain at work.
-Reuter

label: text
text: Safety Men Remaining. London, Oct. 12.

label: text
text: The delegate conference of safety men in London unanimously adopted a resolution reaffirming their decision to remain at work. Reuter.

The Nationalist Government has received a telegram from General Tang Sang-chee at Han-kow confirming the capture of Wuchang by troops of the 4th and 8th Nationalist Armies at 3.30 a.m. of Oct. 10.
A council of war had decided that the historic city should be captured at all costs on the anniversary of the Revolution, that great transaction having started at Wuchang on October 10.

label: text

Before the Debacle.
Developments prior to the "surrender of Wuchang are recorded in the following report to the "China Press":—

label: text
text:
Hankow, Oct. '8.
Your correspondent was the first person to enter Wuchang in 35 days and he found a pitiful state of affairs with the streets peopled only by corpses lying unburied in the roadways.

label: text
text: Shops and dwellings were barred, with here and there a few gathered around a doorstep, their faces showing the privations they had been through, though strangely enough they were more hungry for news than for food.

label: text
text: The food situation has eased somewhat during the past few days owing to the departure of the refugees and to the decision of the defenders to go over to the Kuomintang, for it is now openly declared that a peace pact was signed yesterday and that Liu Yu-chun with 4,000 of his troops will be incorporated in the southern army while the other 8,000 disarmed and disbanded.

label: text
text: “The prevailing opinion is that the gates of Wuchang will be thrown open to the southerners on October 10, that being the “double—ten” day marking the inauguration of the Chinese Republic.

label: text
text: More About Methods. Here is further intelligence about modern methods in China's war:—

label: text
text: It was the southern army which first used airplanes effectively in the present civil war but this weapon has now been turned against them.

label: text
text: The arrival at the front of recent reinforcements from the north equipped with steel helmets and several other innovations caused a great sensation.

label: text
text: Military observers say that hotels can be of little use in the present mode of Chinese warfare because there is little or no shrapnel. The foreign business element in Shanghai is unanimously pleased at the prospect of defeat for the southerners because they fear a repetition of the Hong Kong boycott in Shanghai.—“United Press.”

label: paragraph_title
text: Northerners Were Too Tired to

label: text
text: The southern troops in the district of Kao-an have retreated of their own accord. Those southerners who have been holding their own on the shores of the Shiusui River have been defeated and are also beating retreat.

label: text
text: The allied troops having sustained a great loss, apparently have no strength to pursue the southerners any further. With the exception of battle fronts on the shores of the Shiusui River, no fierce fighting is taking place in other sectors.

label: text
text: Under these circumstances, unless General Chang Kai-shek takes the offensive, it appears no decisive battle will take place in the near future.

label: text
text: It is true, however, that politicians are becoming more active than ever and the prospects are that an end will be put to the present warfare through political means.—Toho.

label: text
text: It is learned here that Marshal Sun Chuan-fang's forces are retreating towards Nanchang and Kiukiang.

label: text
text: As a consequence of shooting upon river steamers by soldiers on both banks of the river between Hwangchow and Yochen, several steamers now are anchoring at Hwangshihkan, Wuyu, and Chichow instead of running further risks. Kuo Wen.

label: text
text: As was stated, the boycott has been settled and certain views are still held but Canton needs the trade for the revenue.

label: text
text: Now as to the definite moves towards resumption, further progress has been recorded.

label: text
text: This morning, a shipment of foreign blankets, in bales, went up to Canton, most probably as a "feeler." No anxiety is entertained as to the cargo being cleared from ship on arrival in Canton, and to the goods reaching the ultimate buyer.

label: text

Cargo from North.
Owing to delay by the weather, the Indo-China Co.'s "Hopsang" did not leave for Canton this morning—having only just arrived—but will sell to-morrow.

label: text
text: Another Jardine boat going up to-morrow is the s.s. "Yatshing." Both these steamers are taking cargo from Shanghai and North China, thereby resuming the round-trip trade of pre-strike days. Cargo is also being loaded at Hong Kong for Canton.

label: text
text: Had it not been for the misunderstanding at Swatow, the Douglas Co. may have resumed the call there already. As it is, the bosta of this line may go to Swatow next week.

label: text
text:
Macao-Canton Boat.
Another step forward is the resumption of communication between Macao and Canton.

label: text
text: The s.s. "Shing Cheong" left Macao for Canton this morning and the "Hang Cheong" sails to-morrow, taking up the day run—one each way per day—as martial law at Bocca Tigris prevents night passage.

label: text
text: "The tow-boat from Macao will also leave for Kongmoon so soon as overhaul to the launch is completed."

label: text
text: Yesterday the "three steam launches from Nam Tau (in Deep Bay, on the other side of the New Territory) brought 110 passengers to Hong Kong, a vast improvement on the handful of a week ago.

label: text
text: The “China Mail” has already reported the resumption—as from to-morrow—of the tow-boat from Hong Kong to Shekki. The Taiping and Kowkong tow-boats are also going back.

label: text
text: When the China Navigation Co.'s "Fatshan" returned yesterday, she had about 800 passengers. This is considerably more than the highest strike total.

label: text
text: The quantity of cargo was also encouraging. On board were a number of passengers who are believed to have been formerly employed by the Tung On. S.S. Co., who are now trying to regain their old positions.

label: text
text:
Wharves Next Week?
The "Sai On" arrived in Canton yesterday without incident. The company is engaged in dredging that part of the river where their wharf lies and it is expected that the wharf will be used in another three days. The "Tung On" is going up on Sunday.

label: text
text: Several of the A.P.C. staff left Hong Kong yesterday for Canton and business is to be resumed now at that port and up the West River. The B.A.T. Co. has also taken steps to supply the Canton and up-country market again with their products.

label: text
text: Passengers by "Railway to Canton yesterday were fewer owing to the competition of the "Sal On."

label: paragraph_title
text: SLAVERY IN NEPAL

label: paragraph_title
text: COMPLETE ABOLITION.

label: text
text: Allahabad.—The Pioneer's Nepal correspondent states that an official statement issued at Katmandu shows that the Maharaja's anti-slavery campaign has triumphantly concluded with the manumission of 57,889 slaves, and that slavery no longer exists in Nepal. The emancipation started early last year. It was carefully planned and proceeded smoothly, the owners co-operating in a, notable manner. Out of a total of 15,719 owners the large majority favoured immediate release, and under 500 of them opposed abolition. Over 1,200 offered liberation without compensation, and actually freed 4,651 slaves without any cost to the Government.

label: text
text: The Maharaja's humanitarian policy has cost the Nepalese Government over 86 jakhs of rupees (about £240,000), the rate of compensation averaging seventy rupees per slave. The scheduled rates ranged from fifteen rupees ten annas for a male baby under 8 to a maximum of 100 rupees for an able-bodied woman aged 18 to 40, the female price averaging over 80 per cent more than the male.

label: text
text: With the object of providing a livelihood for the manumitted people cultivable lands have been thrown open and reclamation and clearance work has been started in Terai. Arrangements are in hand for the issue of sufficient advances to enable the newly-freed people to earn their living.

label: paragraph_title
text: EUROPEANS DEATH IN SINGAPORE.

label: text
text: VERDICT AT INQUEST.

label: text
text: [From Our Own Correspondent.] Singapore October 12

label: text
text:
Singapore, October 12.
A verdict of death by misadventure was returned at the inquestion Mr. A. W. Robertson, who fell from the Europe Hotel window with fatal results.

label: paragraph_title
text: Story of Tragedy.

label: text
text:
The news of the tragedy was called at the time by our Singapore correspondent: Early on the morning of October 5, Mr. A. W. Robertson, the manager of Johore Rubber Lands, Sungei Platong, fell from the window of his room on the top floor of the Hotel, facing High Street, Singapore, and was killed.
In falling he struck the telephone wires, which were broken, and sustained terrible injuries to his head and body.

label: text
text: It is known that Mr. Robertson returned to the Hotel at about 1 a.m. and until 2 a.m. was with n friend in the Hotel.

label: text
text: No one saw him fall, but a watchman found his body in the street at five o'clock. The watchman called Mr. G. Goldsack, assistant manager of the Europe Hotel, and Dr. Rattray was subsequently called and pronounced life extinct. Outside Mr. Robertson's room there was a three-foot opening, and the room was 60 feet from the ground. Mr. Robertson took over the managership of Johore Rubber Lands in June of this year. He had had a wide planting experience and was a well-known planter. In 1911, he was assistant manager of Chembong estate, and joined Sun Bctong estate in 1912 as manager.
